items.stem: Describe the explosive conditions prevailed in Balkans after 1871 in Europe.
items.answer: After 1871 the Balkans became the most explosive region of Europe. The Balkans was a region of great geographical and ethnic variation, covering modern Romania, Bulgaria, Albania, Greece, Macedonia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia, Serbia and Montenegro, whose inhabitants were broadly known as the Slavs. Much of the area was under Ottoman rule, and through the nineteenth century the Ottoman Empire tried to strengthen itself by modernisation and internal reform but with very little success. One by one its European subject nationalities broke away from its control and declared themselves independent. These Balkan peoples based their claims to independence and political rights on nationality, using history to prove that they had once been independent and had later been subjugated by foreign powers. Each rebellious nationality therefore saw its struggle as an attempt to win back a long lost independence, and as the various Slavic groups fought one another over territory, and the big European powers backed rival claims in the race for trade, colonies and naval strength, the region was converted into a battleground.

items.stem: Illustrate with examples that food offers many opportunities of long-distance cultural exchange.
items.answer: Food shows very clearly how distant cultures have exchanged with one another. Traders and travellers introduced new crops to every land they reached, so that ready foodstuff in distant parts of the world often share a common origin. Many of our commonest foods — potatoes, maize, soya, groundnuts, tomatoes, chillies and sweet potatoes — came to Europe and Asia from the Americas, and were unknown to our ancestors until about five centuries ago. It is believed that noodles travelled west from China to become 'spaghetti', or perhaps Arab traders carried pasta to fifth century Sicily, an island in Italy. Indian 'rotis' have become 'tortillas' in Mexico, America and other western countries. Similar foods were also known in India and Japan, so the truth about their origin may never be settled, yet the very guesswork suggests how much long-distance cultural contact there was even in the pre-modern world. The consequences could be dramatic: with the introduction of the potato Europe's poor began to eat better and live longer, and the poor of Ireland became so dependent on it that when disease destroyed the potato crop in the 1840s a large number of people died of starvation. Food, therefore, is one of the clearest records of long-distance cultural exchange.

items.stem: “Even before factories began to dot the landscape in England and Europe, there was large-scale industrial production for an international market in the country side.” Elucidate.
items.answer: The seventeenth and eighteenth centuries were a time when open fields were disappearing and commons were being enclosed. Cottagers and poor peasants who had earlier depended on common land for survival — gathering firewood, berries, vegetables, hay and straw — now had to look for alternative sources of income. Many had only tiny plots of land that could not employ all the members of the household, so when merchants arrived and offered advances to produce goods for them, they happily agreed. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries merchants from the towns of Europe began moving to the countryside, supplying money to peasants and artisans and persuading them to produce for an international market. With the expansion of world trade and the acquisition of colonies in different parts of the world the demand for goods was growing, but merchants could not expand production within the towns because urban crafts and trade guilds were powerful there. The guilds were associations of producers that trained craftspeople, maintained control over production, regulated competition and prices and restricted the entry of new people into a trade, and rulers had granted different guilds the monopoly right to produce and trade in specific products, so it was very difficult for a new merchant to set up business in a town. This is why merchants turned to the countryside, where poor peasants and artisans who had lost their common lands began working for them. In this way large-scale industrial production for an international market was already being carried on in the villages, long before factories dotted the landscape.

items.stem: “The function and the shape of the family were completely transformed by life in the industrial city.” Clarify the statement with regard to urbanization that happened in England in the 18th century.
items.answer: In the eighteenth century the family had been a unit of production and of consumption as well as of political decision-making, and life in the industrial city broke that older pattern completely. Ties between members of the household loosened, and among the working class the institution of marriage tended to break down. Women of the upper and middle classes in Britain, on the other hand, faced increasingly higher levels of isolation, although their lives were made easier by domestic maids who cooked, cleaned and cared for young children on low wages. Women who worked for wages did gain some control over their own lives, particularly among the lower social classes; but many social reformers felt that the family as an institution had broken down and needed to be saved or reconstructed by pushing these women back into their homes. The city also encouraged a new spirit of individualism among both men and women and a freedom from the collective values that had been a feature of the smaller rural communities. Men and women, however, did not have equal access to this new urban space: as women lost their industrial jobs and conservative people rallied against their presence in public places, women were forced to withdraw into their homes. Thus both the function and the shape of the family were transformed by the industrial city.

items.stem: Describe any five factors that led to the end of the Bretton Woods system and the beginning of globalisation.
items.answer: The Bretton Woods system came apart for several connected reasons. First, from the 1960s the rising costs of its overseas involvements weakened the finances and the competitive strength of the United States. Second, the US dollar no longer commanded confidence as the world's principal currency. Third, the dollar could not maintain its fixed value in relation to gold, which was the anchor of the whole arrangement. Fourth, this eventually led to the collapse of the system of fixed exchange rates and to the introduction of a system of floating exchange rates. Fifth, the international financial system itself changed in important ways: developing countries were now forced to borrow from western commercial banks and private lending institutions instead of from the Bretton Woods institutions, which brought periodic debt crises and lower incomes. Finally, the industrial world was hit by unemployment, and multinational companies began shifting production to low-wage countries, above all to China, whose cheap labour made it a favoured destination. Together these developments ended the Bretton Woods order and opened the era of globalisation.

items.stem: Explain the statement ‘the food travels throughout the world’ with examples.
items.answer: That food travels throughout the world is a historical fact. Trade in goods, including foodgrains, always carried long-distance cultural exchange with it: traders and travellers introduced new crops to the lands they visited, so that even rare foodstuffs in far apart parts of the world may share a common origin. Spaghetti and noodles are the standard example — it is believed that noodles travelled west from China to become spaghetti, or perhaps Arab traders took pasta to fifth century Sicily, an island now in Italy. Similar foods were also known in India and Japan, and are so ancient there that their origins may never be established; such guesswork itself suggests the possibilities of long-distance cultural contact even in the pre-modern world. Many of our common foods — potatoes, soya, groundnuts, maize, tomatoes, chillies and sweet potatoes — were not known to our ancestors until about five centuries ago. They were introduced into Europe and Asia only after Christopher Columbus incidentally discovered the vast continent later known as the Americas, including North America, South America and the Caribbean. Food therefore travels with people, and the world's kitchens are a record of that travel.

items.stem:
Why has the indentured labour system in 19th century been described as a new system of slavery ?
or
Nineteenth century indenture has been described on a new system of slavery. Explain three reasons.
items.answer: Nineteenth century indenture is called a new system of slavery because, although the labourer signed a contract, in practice he was bound and exploited much as a slave was. It was a world of faster economic growth but also of greater misery — higher incomes for some and poverty for others, technological advance in some areas and new forms of exploitation in others. Most indentured workers migrated in the hope of a bright future, but they were exploited both by the recruiting agent and by the employer. They had to pay a commission to the recruiting agent out of their meagre earnings. The agents routinely gave false information about the final destination, the modes of travel, the nature of the work and the living and working conditions, so that the worker agreed to terms he did not understand. Sometimes agents even forcibly abducted less willing migrants. Once on the plantation the worker's legal rights were minimal and he could not leave before the contract ended. For all these reasons the system, though formally contractual, amounted to a new form of slavery.

items.stem: Write any three factors responsible for indentured labour migration from India.
items.answer: Indentured labour was bonded labour working under contract for an employer for a specified period, and several factors pushed such migration out of India. First, the world order of the time was one of domination and slavery: Europeans grew steadily wealthier while the people of Asian and African countries suffered misery, exploitation and poverty at the same time. Second, the colonial economy at home was collapsing — cottage industries in India declined, rates of land revenue rose, and peasants were displaced by Europeans setting up large-scale industries; these pressures forced Indian peasants to migrate to other countries as indentured labourers. Third, there was a strong pull from abroad, because the demand for labour was high in Trinidad, Guyana and Surinam in the Caribbean and in Mauritius and Fiji, where plantations needed cheap workers. This produced a large-scale flow of labour from the East to the West, and a contract labour system emerged in which middlemen, of the kind already seen in the slave trade, recruited and controlled the workers, as was plain from the behaviour of British plantation owners and miners towards indentured labourers during the contract period.

items.stem: How was the food problem solved in Britain after the scrapping of the ‘Corn Laws’ ? Explain.
items.answer: After the Corn Laws were scrapped, Britain solved its food problem in three ways. First, foodgrains and other eatables were imported. Once the restriction was gone, foodgrains and all kinds of food items were brought in from abroad, and they were cheaper than anything that could be produced within Britain; British traders and merchants began importing cheap food from Australia, the USA, Russia and some eastern European countries. Second, a new shape was given to the agricultural economy. A global agricultural economy took hold, for the large-scale import of foodgrains made food a world commodity: food no longer came from a nearby town or village but from thousands of miles away. In the exporting regions large farms were created and cultivated with new agricultural machines and tools, and these farms were linked to the ports by railways, roads and waterways. Third, networks of irrigation were built in Britain's colonies: the British colonial government in India and elsewhere constructed networks of irrigation canals that transformed semi-desert wastes into fertile agricultural land capable of growing wheat and cotton for export to Britain. In this way cheap food from a world-wide supply area replaced the protected home supply.

items.stem: Discuss the main characteristics related with First World Wartime transformation.
items.answer: The First World War transformed the world in several basic ways. It was the first modern industrial war, born of the industrial interests of the big powers, and it saw machine guns, tanks, aircraft and chemical weapons used on a massive scale. It caused a great shortage of men of working age, because most of those killed and injured were men of working age, and these deaths and injuries reduced the able-bodied workforce of Europe. It brought women workers into the service and industrial sectors: industries were restructured to produce war-related goods, entire societies were reorganised for war, and as men went to battle women stepped into jobs in factories, offices, schools and hospitals. Finally, it reversed the financial standing of the great powers — Britain became a debtor and the United States became an international creditor. The war shattered markets, the agricultural production Europeans had earlier maintained slumped, and money had to be borrowed from American banks and the American public. These are the main characteristics of the wartime transformation.

items.stem: How did the First World War change the economic life of the people in Britain ? Explain.
items.answer: The First World War had a great impact on the economic life of Britain. First, there was heavy expenditure: Britain had to fight on several fronts and bore very heavy costs during the war years, so post-war economic recovery proved very difficult and the war weakened the British economy. Second, Britain faced new industrial competition. While she was preoccupied with the war, industries had developed in Japan and India, and Britain now had to face competition from these countries, especially from Japan. Third, there was a heavy loan burden owed to the USA: to finance war expenditure Britain had borrowed liberally from the United States, so that at the end of the war she was burdened with huge external debts. Fourth, economic depression followed. Prices of most commodities had risen during the war; afterwards several industrial units closed down, unemployment increased and exports of many items fell. Some banks, insurance companies and financial institutions were forced to declare themselves bankrupt under the adverse impact of the Economic Depression that came out of the USA between 1929 and 1933. Together these changes left the British people poorer, more indebted and more exposed to unemployment than before the war.

items.stem: What do you know about World Trade Organisation? Explain.
items.answer: The World Trade Organisation (WTO) was set up under the United Nations to promote international trade among countries, and its headquarters is at Geneva. It was established on 1 January 1995 and by January 2002 had 144 member countries; India became a member on 1 January 1995. The WTO replaced the General Agreement on Trade and Tariffs (GATT), which had been established in 1948. It has significantly influenced the process of liberalisation in the world. The organisation is based on the principle of discrimination-free trade and the promotion of fair competition among member nations. Most of its rules are framed on the basis of persuasion and its decisions are taken by consensus; the Ministerial Conference is its law-making body, though the USA has considerable hegemony there. The WTO wants both import and export quotas to be abolished and wants countries to follow multinational agreements, and all its members have adopted laws and policies in order to comply with WTO rules.

items.stem: Why liberalisation has been adopted in India ? Mention freedoms given to private sector under it. Also enlist main measures undertaken for liberalisation of economy in our country since 1991.
items.answer: India adopted liberalisation to achieve three objectives: to free Indian industry from needless and irksome controls, to upgrade technology, and to develop international competitiveness. The freedoms given to the private sector under liberalisation were these: industrial licensing was abolished except for five priority industries; the number of public sector industries was reduced from 17 to 3; and industry was freed from regulations such as the need for permission to import raw materials. The main measures undertaken for the liberalisation of the Indian economy since 1991 were the abolition of industrial licensing and registration, concessions from the Monopolies Act, freedom for industries to expand and to raise production, an increase in the investment limit of small industries, freedom to import capital goods, freedom to import technology, and free determination of interest rates. Taken together these steps replaced a permit-based economy with one in which the private sector chose its own scale, technology and markets.

items.stem: Describe the main changes that took place due to Liberalisation and Globalisation.
items.answer: The changes brought by liberalisation and globalisation can be classified into visible changes and invisible changes. The visible changes were felt directly by consumers: far better services in the telecommunication sector, and colour television sets and other electronic goods available at low prices; and the market for cold drinks and food products being taken over by companies such as Pepsi and Coca-Cola. The invisible changes were structural. India's share in the world trade of goods and services increased. Investment from foreign countries rose sharply, from ₹174 crores in 1991 to ₹9,338 crores in 2000, and foreign exchange needed to pay for imports grew from ₹4,822 crores in 1991 to ₹1,59,924 crores in 2000. New jobs were created, but not in sufficient numbers to meet all the needs, especially in the rural sector, and the growth of industry did not reach the level that had been expected. Thus liberalisation and globalisation brought visible consumer gains along with mixed results for employment and industrial growth.

items.stem: Describe any five measures of liberalisation taken by the Government of India.
items.answer: The Government of India took the following measures of liberalisation. First, industries were exempted from licensing: the private sector has been freed to set up all industries except a few, without any kind of industrial licence. Second, permission was given to import raw material from abroad — under the new economic policy companies can import raw materials and government permission is no longer required. Third, the investment limit of small industries was extended, the restriction on investment by large business having been lifted. Fourth, the concept of MRTP was done away with, so that there are now no MRTP companies and firms can take their own investment decisions and expansion plans. Fifth, industries were allowed to expand freely according to the needs of the market, the ceiling on capital having been abolished. Sixth, the number of industries reserved for the public sector was reduced from 7 to 3, so that the private sector can now enter core industries such as iron and steel, electricity, air transport, shipbuilding, heavy machinery and some defence goods.

items.stem: What was the main aim of the post-war international economic system? Mention the two Bretton Woods Institutions established in 1944 with their main objectives.
items.answer: The main aim of the post-war international economic system was to preserve economic stability and full employment in the industrial world. Economists and politicians had drawn two key lessons from inter-war economic experience. First, an industrial society is based on mass consumption. Second, to ensure mass consumption there had to be high and stable incomes, and incomes could not be stable unless employment was stable; thus stable incomes also require steady, full employment. Since markets alone could not guarantee full employment, governments would have to step in to minimise fluctuations of price, output and employment, so that economic stability could be ensured only through the intervention of the government. The framework of this programme was agreed upon at the United Nations Monetary and Financial Conference held in July 1944 at Bretton Woods in New Hampshire, USA. Two institutions were established there: the International Monetary Fund, whose objective was to deal with the external surpluses and deficits of its member nations, and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, the World Bank, set up to finance post-war reconstruction. The Bretton Woods system inaugurated an era of unprecedented growth of trade and income for the western industrial nations and Japan.

items.stem:
‘G-77 can be seen as a reaction to the activities of Bretton Woods Twins’. Explain the statement with three arguments.
or
Describe the circumstances responsible for the formation of G-77.
items.answer: It is rightly said that the G-77 can be seen as a reaction to the activities of the Bretton Woods twins. The Bretton Woods twins, the IMF and the World Bank, were dominated by the former colonial powers, so most developing countries did not benefit from the fast growth that the western economies experienced in the 1950s and 1960s; they therefore organised themselves as a group, the Group of 77 or G-77, to demand a New International Economic Order. The former colonial powers continued to exploit the natural resources of developing nations through the IMF and the World Bank, and the developing nations organised themselves into the G-77 so as to gain real control over their own natural resources. They also wanted more developmental assistance and fairer prices for the raw materials they sold, and a better opportunity for their manufactured goods in the markets of the developed nations. The G-77 was thus the collective answer of the newly independent countries to an international economic order that had been built without them.

items.stem: ‘The impact of Great Depression of 1929 was different on the Indian rural and industrial society.’ Justify the statement.
items.answer: The Great Depression of 1929 struck India, then under British rule, severely, but it fell very unevenly on the countryside and on the towns. The Government of British India adopted a protective trade policy which, though beneficial for the United Kingdom, caused great damage to the Indian economy. During 1929-1937 exports and imports fell drastically, crippling seaborne international trade, and the railways and the agricultural sector were the worst affected. Peasants and farmers suffered far more than urban dwellers: although agricultural prices fell sharply, the colonial government refused to reduce its revenue demands, and peasants producing for the world market were hit hardest of all. Across India peasants' indebtedness increased; they used up their savings, mortgaged their lands and sold jewellery and precious metals to meet daily expenses. For urban India, on the other hand, the depression was far less grim precisely because prices were falling. Those with fixed incomes — town-dwelling landowners who received rents and middle class salaried employees — found themselves better off, since everything cost less, and they also benefited from industrial investment, which grew because the government had extended tariff protection to industries. Thus the same depression ruined the rural producer while leaving urban India comparatively better placed.
